WHEN LIFE INTERRUPTS THE MUSIC; Series 4 Returning With a Different Perspective Sometimes, you return to the place you left, but you are no longer the person who left. Coming Home With “Nothing” I did not plan the return. There was no carefully prepared timeline. No grand announcement. No sense that everything had worked out exactly as I had hoped. It was sudden, unplanned, and, at the time, it felt almost like the end. After a long period of labour and a series of unpleasant experiences, I found myself going back home with what, from the outside, looked like nothing. No significant achievement to announce. No great story of success. No evidence that things had gone according to plan. Just me, returning home. I remember the feeling. There is a particular kind of disappointment that comes when reality does not resemble the picture you had imagined. You leave home believing you are going to build something. You worked, endured, and made sacrifices. You keep hoping. And then, unexpectedly, you find yourself coming back, wondering what exactly you have to show for the journey. But something happened when I arrived home that I did not expect. My Children Were There. They were shocked. Then excited. My wife was happy to see me. And in the middle of everything I had been carrying, something shifted. For a moment, I wasn’t thinking about what I had lost. I wasn’t thinking about what had gone wrong. I wasn’t thinking about what I had hoped to accomplish. I was simply home. And there was a little joy in that. It was not the kind of joy that solved every problem. It did not suddenly change my circumstances. But it reminded me of something I had perhaps allowed the pursuit of other things to overshadow: There are things more valuable than the achievements we spend our lives chasing. Sometimes, Coming Home Is Not Going Back Before that experience, I might have looked at returning home as simply moving backwards. But I began to see it differently. I was not returning as the same person who had left. I had experiences I did not have before. I had been tested in ways I had not anticipated. I had encountered uncertainty. I had experienced rejection. I had learned to function in unfamiliar circumstances. I had discovered things about myself. And perhaps most importantly, I had developed a different understanding of what really matters. So although the return looked like a setback, I was carrying something home with me that could not be seen in a suitcase. Perspective. Experience. Wisdom. Humility. Resilience. And a deeper appreciation for family. The Season Was Heavy The months that followed were not easy. I was given one month notice to evacuation where I was staying with my family. There were days of uncertainty. There were disappointments. There were moments when rejection made me question what was next. There were times when I had to confront the emotional weight of everything that had happened. My blood pressure rose up. I also had to navigate other difficult personal seasons that affected me physically and emotionally. There were moments when the pressure felt overwhelming. Some came from people who were supposed to encourage and support me at my down moment. But somewhere along the way, I came to a realisation: I am too loaded to give up now. I don’t mean that life suddenly became easy. It didn’t. I mean that I had accumulated too much experience, too many lessons, too much responsibility, too much love, too much purpose, and too much understanding to allow one difficult chapter to become the conclusion of my story. I had people depending on me. I had people I had influenced. I had things I still wanted to contribute. I had lessons that had cost me something to learn. And I began to understand that survival itself can sometimes be an act of courage. My Perspective About Family Changed Coming home changed the way I looked at family. Sometimes, we can become so focused on providing, achieving, building, and pursuing that we forget that the people we are building for are also part of the reward. Coming home and seeing my children again reminded me that presence has value. Not everything meaningful can be measured by income. Not everything important can be displayed as an achievement. Sometimes, sitting with your family after a difficult season is itself a victory. My wife’s happiness at seeing me reminded me that partnership is not only about celebrating success together. Sometimes, it is about having someone who is simply glad that you are home. That changed something in me. My Perspective About Music Changed My relationship with music also changed. Before, I could easily think about music in terms of achievement, performance, growth, opportunities, and professional development. But after everything I had experienced, music began to feel deeper. I began to see it not merely as something I do, but as something through which I can serve, teach, communicate, influence, encourage, and connect with people. I became more interested in the person behind the musician. What does music do to someone’s confidence? How does training shape discipline? How can a teacher help a young person discover potential? How can leadership develop people rather than simply produce performances? These questions became more important to me. My experiences had changed the questions I asked. And sometimes, a change in the questions is evidence that growth has already begun. My Perspective About Leadership Changed Leadership also began to look different. I had previously thought a lot about building. Building teams. Building musicians. Building programmes. Building curriculums. Building platforms. But difficult seasons taught me something about leadership that success cannot always teach: People need leaders who understand what it means to struggle. You cannot always lead from a position of strength. Sometimes you lead while rebuilding. Sometimes you encourage others while you are still finding your own footing. Sometimes you have to admit that you don’t have all the answers. Sometimes leadership is simply refusing to surrender your responsibility to hope. That experience gave me greater empathy for people who are struggling silently. I became less interested in judging people’s seasons and more interested in understanding them. Rejection Does Not Have to Become Identity One of the difficult things about rejection is that it can become personal. An opportunity is rejected, and we begin to think we are rejected. A plan fails, and we begin to think we are failures. A door closes, and we begin to believe there are no more doors. I had to learn to separate an experience from my identity. A rejection is an event. It is not necessarily a definition. A difficult season is a season. It is not necessarily a destination. A failed plan is a failed plan. It does not automatically mean a failed person. That distinction became important as I began rebuilding. I Had to Learn to Live Without Having Everything Figured Out There is a pressure many adults carry—the pressure to know what comes next. We want the plan, the timeline, the certainty, the answer. But life does not always give us those things. Sometimes you have to take the next step without seeing the entire road. That was one of the lessons this season taught me. I could not control everything that had happened. I could not immediately control what would happen next. But I could control how I responded. I could keep learning, working, showing up, loving my family, developing people, keep creating and believing that the story was not finished. That was enough for the next step. I Came Back, But I Did Not Come Back Empty This is perhaps the biggest lesson of this chapter. I initially thought I was coming home with “nothing” But I eventually realised I was carrying a lot. I came back with experience. I came back with stories. I came back with lessons. I came back with a deeper appreciation for family. I came back with a different understanding of leadership. I came back with a broader perspective on people. I came back with greater resilience. I came back with a clearer understanding of what matters. And I came back with a renewed appreciation for the gift of music. Perhaps I did not return with everything I wanted. But I returned with something I needed: Perspective . The Person Who Left Is Not the Person Who Returned This is what I want to emphasize most. Sometimes we define success by what we bring back. The money. The position. The certificate. The business. The opportunity. The achievement. But perhaps we should also ask: Who did the journey make you? Because sometimes, you return with fewer possessions but greater wisdom. You return with fewer answers but better questions. You return with fewer plans but greater clarity. You return with less certainty but greater resilience. You return thinking you have lost something, only to discover that you have gained a deeper understanding of yourself. That was my experience. And Now, Another Birthday As I celebrate my birthday today, October 5, I find myself reflecting differently on the journey. I don’t want to pretend that I have arrived. I haven’t. There are still things I am working toward. There are still questions I don’t have answers to. There are still areas of my life that require growth. There are still dreams waiting for expression. But I can say one thing with honesty: I am not the same person I used to be. And perhaps that is worth celebrating. Not because everything is perfect. Not because every prayer has been answered. Not because every plan has worked. But because I am still here. Still learning. Still building. Still loving. Still teaching. Still creating. Still dreaming. Still becoming. I May Not Be There Yet I have learned to appreciate this sentence: “I may not be there yet.” There is humility in it. But there is also hope. It means I recognise the distance between where I am and where I want to be. It means I refuse to pretend. But it also means I haven’t given up. I may not be where I thought I would be by now. But I am not where I used to be. And that matters. Growth is not always dramatic. Sometimes it is simply becoming more intentional, more patient, more aware, more grateful, more resilient, more responsible, more compassionate, more willing to learn, more comfortable with the process. The Lesson I Carry Forward If the past few years have taught me anything, it is this: Life can interrupt your plans without destroying your purpose. You can lose an opportunity and still find yourself. You can return home and still move forward. You can experience rejection and still have value. You can go through an unfamiliar season and still develop capacity. You can feel like you have nothing and still be carrying something priceless. And sometimes, the person who emerges from the difficult season is better equipped for the next chapter than the person who entered it. “Sometimes, returning is not going back. It is coming home with a perspective that only the journey could have given you.”— Victor Adenola A Reflection for You Perhaps you are also in a season that doesn’t look like what you planned. Maybe you have had to return. Maybe something you built has ended. Maybe an opportunity didn’t work out. Maybe you have experienced rejection. Maybe you are rebuilding. Maybe you feel as though you have very little to show for the years you have invested. Please don’t be too quick to measure your life only by what you can show. Ask yourself: What has the journey built inside me? What have I learned? How have I changed? What capacity have I developed? Who have I become? Who have I influenced? What do I understand now that I didn’t understand before? Because sometimes, the greatest evidence that a season was not wasted is not what you acquired. It is who you became. And as I celebrate another year, that is where I find some of my gratitude. I may not be where I want to be. But I am not where I used to be. And I am still becoming. Coming Next — Series 5: When the Music Plays Again After the pause, the interruption, the unfamiliar season, the ending, the return, and the lessons, one question remains: What happens when you are ready to play again? Perhaps the goal is not to recreate the music exactly as it was before. Perhaps the next movement requires everything the journey has taught you. In Series 5, I reflect on new beginnings, intentionality, purpose, family, music, and the courage to begin again—not as the person you were, but as the person you have become. #commitment #consistency #courage #creativity #EmotionalWellBeing #Intentionality #musicians #performance #Purpose #retreat #Victoradenola
